lemma: Suffix-separation lemma (deterministic, conditional on a collision). For every n≥1 and distinct u,v∈{0,1}^n, define y=u∧¬v if u∧¬v≠0, and otherwise y=v∧¬u. Then exactly one of u,v is disjoint from y. Consequently, for any deterministic one-pass streaming algorithm A whose states after u and v are equal, A gives the same answer on (u,y) and (v,y), although their DISJ answers differ, so A errs on at least one of these two inputs. Proof: In the first case, y has a 1 only where u has a 1 and v has a 0; hence u intersects y and v is disjoint from y. In the second case u∧¬v=0, so every 1 of u is also a 1 of v. Since u≠v, v∧¬u≠0; y is then disjoint from u and intersects v. Equal streaming states after the prefixes, followed by the same suffix, yield equal final states and outputs. This proves only suffix construction once a collision is supplied; it does not uniformly select a colliding pair or address randomized algorithms.
gap: Open: construct, for every admissible deterministic streaming algorithm in Q-30931971e1, a pair of distinct colliding prefixes selected by a polylogtime-uniform AC0 family without advice (and resolve the randomized case). The suffix-separation lemma is conditional on already having such a pair.

proved_step:
statement: For every n≥1 and distinct u,v∈{0,1}^n, let y=u∧¬v if u∧¬v≠0; otherwise let y=v∧¬u. Exactly one of u,v is disjoint from y. Thus, if a deterministic one-pass streaming algorithm has the same state after u and v, it gives the same output on (u,y) and (v,y), although their DISJ answers differ, so it errs on at least one.
proof: If u∧¬v≠0, every 1-coordinate of y has u_i=1 and v_i=0; hence u intersects y and v is disjoint from y. Otherwise u_i≤v_i for every i. Since u≠v, some coordinate has v_i=1 and u_i=0, so y=v∧¬u is nonzero, u is disjoint from y, and v intersects y. In either case the two DISJ answers differ. Equal deterministic states after the prefixes, followed by the same suffix, produce the same final state and output.

statement: For every n≥1 and fixed omitted coordinate i(n)∈[n], let σ_n(x)=x with coordinate i(n) deleted. The prefixes u_n=0^n and v_n=e_{i(n)} collide under σ_n, and the common suffix y_n=e_{i(n)} gives DISJ(u_n,y_n)=1 and DISJ(v_n,y_n)=0. If i(n) is computable by a polylogtime-uniform AC0 family (in particular, if i(n)=1), these prefix and suffix families are uniformly AC0-constructible.
proof: Deleting coordinate i(n) makes u_n and v_n identical on every retained coordinate, so σ_n(u_n)=σ_n(v_n). The all-zero string is disjoint from y_n, while v_n=e_{i(n)} intersects y_n at coordinate i(n), giving opposite DISJ answers. The construction outputs zeros or the unit vector at i(n); under the stated uniformity assumption these strings are generated by the corresponding uniform AC0 family.

statement: Fix an integer q>=1 and a deterministic one-pass streaming machine A with at most q states. For each n>=q and j in {0,...,q}, let x_j(n)=1^j0^(n-j). Then there is a fixed pair 0<=a<b<=q such that A reaches the same state after x_a(n) and x_b(n) for infinitely many n. Each of the two prefix families is polylogtime-uniform AC0 constructible. For those infinitely many n, the suffix-separation lemma supplies a common suffix on which the two DISJ answers differ.
proof: For each n>=q, the q+1 prefixes x_0(n),...,x_q(n) lead to at most q states. Thus some pair (a_n,b_n) with a_n<b_n collides. There are only binom(q+1,2) possible pairs. If each pair collided at only finitely many n, the union of those finite sets of lengths would be finite, contradicting that a colliding pair exists for every n>=q. Hence one fixed pair (a,b) collides for infinitely many n. For fixed a, x_a(n) is generated by outputting a initial 1s followed by n-a zeros, which is a uniform AC0 family; likewise for b. At each collision length, apply the suffix-separation lemma to x_a(n),x_b(n). This proves the stated result. The pair depends on A, and this argument does not select it uniformly from A.

evidence: Direct convexity/transfer proof; finite check requested independently in experiment.
proved_step: statement: For integers M>q>=1, every map from an M-element set into a set of at most q states has at least binom(M-q+1,2) unordered colliding pairs. Proof: Let the nonempty fiber sizes be a_1,...,a_r, where r<=q and sum a_i=M. The number of colliding pairs is C=sum_i binom(a_i,2). If two fibers have sizes a>=b>=2, moving one item from the smaller fiber to the larger changes C by binom(a+1,2)+binom(b-1,2)-binom(a,2)-binom(b,2)=a-b+1>=1; hence a minimizing partition has at most one fiber larger than 1. Among at most q fibers this minimum is attained by q-1 singleton fibers and one fiber of size M-q+1, giving C=binom(M-q+1,2). If fewer fibers are used, merging or adding empty fibers does not lower the minimum. This is a counting strengthening of pigeonhole and does not select any colliding pair uniformly from the map.

evidence: Complete balancing proof; the prior discovery counterexample exposed the error in S0004 and motivates the corrected extremal statement.
proved_step: statement: For integers M>=1 and q>=1, the minimum number of unordered colliding pairs over maps from an M-element set into at most q states is (q-r) binom(a,2)+r binom(a+1,2), where a=floor(M/q) and r=M mod q. Proof: Regard the map as q fiber sizes including empty fibers. Its collision count is the sum of binom(a_i,2). If a_i>=a_j+2, replacing these two sizes by a_i-1 and a_j+1 changes the sum by -(a_i-a_j)+1<0. Thus a minimizing q-tuple has sizes differing by at most 1. The sum and number of fibers then force q-r sizes equal to a and r sizes equal to a+1, giving the formula. Such a partition is realized by a map, so this is the minimum. This is a finite counting lemma and does not select a colliding pair uniformly from a machine.

statement: For every q>=1, given as input a table of q+1 binary labels of length ceil(log2 q) representing a map f:{0,...,q}->{0,...,q-1}, a lexicographically first colliding pair can be output by a DLOGTIME-uniform AC0 circuit family of size polynomial in q and log q.
proof: For each pair i<j, compute E_ij=[f(i)=f(j)] by bitwise XNORs followed by an AND over the label bits; this has constant depth. Order the pairs lexicographically and compute S_ij=E_ij AND NOT(OR_{(a,b)<(i,j)} E_ab). These priority gates have constant depth with unbounded fan-in. Pigeonhole guarantees some E_ij=1, so exactly the first colliding pair has S_ij=1. Output each index bit by OR-ing the corresponding bits gated by S_ij. There are O(q^2) pairs, and the gates and wires are generated by regular index comparisons and bit positions, giving polynomial size and DLOGTIME uniformity. The table is an explicit input; this does not generate a streaming machine's table uniformly.

statement: For each integer q>=1, let L=ceil(log2 q) (and L=0 when q=1). Given an explicit table of q+1 labels f(0),...,f(q) in {0,1}^L, one can compute the lexicographically first pair i<j with f(i)=f(j) by a DLOGTIME-uniform AC0 circuit family of size O(q^4+q^2 L) in the standard indexed-table encoding. Proof: For each pair i<j form E_ij as the conjunction, over the L coordinates, of equality literals for the corresponding table bits (for L=0 equality is true). Define P_ij = E_ij AND NOT(OR{E_ab : a<b and (a,b)<lex(i,j)}), with empty OR false. Since q+1 labels take only 2^L<=q values when q>=2, and for q=1 the two zero-bit labels are equal, at least one E_ij is true; exactly the lexicographically first true E_ij has P_ij true. Output each binary index bit as the OR over pairs (i,j) of P_ij gated by that pair's constant index bit. Pairwise equality uses O(L) gates per pair. Building each candidate's priority OR independently uses O(q^4) total gates/wires, so the stated bound follows. Gates and wires are indexed by O(log q)-bit pair and coordinate indices; a DLOGTIME uniformity machine determines the wiring and constants in polylog(q) time. This is an explicit-table selector only; it supplies no circuit for generating or accessing the transition table of an arbitrary streaming algorithm.

refuted_approach: S0007's label-count argument is invalid as stated: ceil(log2 q)-bit strings have 2^ceil(log2 q) possible values, which can exceed q (for example q=3). The pigeonhole conclusion requires a promise that every label encodes an element of {0,...,q-1}. The finite check used modulo-q labels and therefore checked only the promised-domain version. S0007 remains CLAIMED and should not be used as a premise.

proved_step: statement: For every integer q>=1, given an explicit table of q+1 labels, each encoding an element of {0,...,q-1}, a DLOGTIME-uniform AC0 circuit family of size O(q^4+q^2 ceil(log2 q)) outputs the lexicographically first pair i<j with equal labels. Proof: For each pair i<j, compute E_ij, the conjunction of coordinatewise label equality tests. Mark P_ij=E_ij AND NOT(OR of E_ab over all earlier pairs (a,b) in lexicographic order), taking the empty OR as false. Since the q+1 labels take only q possible values, at least one E_ij is true, and exactly the first true pair is marked. For each output index bit, OR the P_ij indicators gated by the corresponding constant bit of i or j. Each pair comparison has O(ceil(log2 q)) size; the independent priority ORs over O(q^2) pairs use O(q^4) size. The table-indexed wiring and constants are DLOGTIME-uniform. This lemma assumes an explicit valid table and gives no uniform generator or access circuit for an arbitrary streaming machine's transition table.

evidence: Constructive parallel selector under the explicit AC0-evaluability hypothesis; this narrows the arbitrary-streaming-machine gap but does not prove the hypothesis for general machines.
proved_step: statement: Let q(n)>=1 be polynomially bounded, and let F_n:{0,...,q(n)}->{0,...,q(n)-1} be a family of state-label maps whose output bits are computed by a DLOGTIME-uniform AC0 family of size poly(n), given the binary index i. Then a DLOGTIME-uniform AC0 family of size poly(n) outputs the lexicographically first pair a<b with F_n(a)=F_n(b). Proof: instantiate q(n)+1 copies of the uniform label circuit on the constant binary indices 0,...,q(n); this has polynomial total size and uniform wiring. For every pair i<j, compute E_ij=[F_n(i)=F_n(j)] using bitwise XNOR and an unbounded-fan-in AND. In parallel compute P_ij=E_ij AND NOT(OR of E_ab over all lexicographically earlier pairs). Pigeonhole guarantees at least one E_ij=1, so exactly the first collision is selected. Output each binary index bit by OR-ing the selected-pair signals whose index has that bit set. The circuit has constant depth and polynomial size; its wiring is DLOGTIME-uniform by the assumed uniformity and regular pair indexing. This is conditional on AC0-evaluability of F_n and does not establish it for arbitrary streaming machines.

statement: Let Q be a fixed set of q states, s0 in Q, and T0,T1:Q->Q fixed transition maps. For every fixed j>=0, the state reached after 1^j0^(n-j), for n>=j, is ultimately periodic in n with preperiod < q and period <= q. Proof: Put z=T1^j(s0). The q+1 states T0^t(z), 0<=t<=q, contain a repetition T0^a(z)=T0^b(z) with 0<=a<b<=q. Applying T0 repeatedly gives T0^(t+b-a)(z)=T0^t(z) for every t>=a. Hence the sequence is periodic from a<q with period b-a<=q. For any fixed finite collection of j values, the tuple of reached states is ultimately periodic, using the maximum of the individual preperiods and the least common multiple of their periods. Consequently, for a fixed machine, state labels on a fixed finite collection of these prefix families are computable by a uniform AC0 family whose constants may depend on the machine. This restricted result does not give a uniform selector for machine families whose transition maps or state counts vary with n.

statement: Let q>=1 be fixed, let Q have q states, and let T0,T1:Q->Q and s0 in Q be fixed. There exist a<b in {0,...,q}, integers mu>=0 and p>=1, such that for every n>=mu with n congruent to mu modulo p, the states reached after 1^a0^(n-a) and 1^b0^(n-b) are equal (restrict to n>=q). Proof: Form the tuple Z_n=(T0^(n-j)(T1^j(s0)))_{j=0}^q in Q^(q+1). For n>=q, Z_(n+1)=U(Z_n), where U applies T0 to every coordinate. This is the orbit of a function U on a set of q^(q+1) tuples. Hence there are mu>=q and p>=1 such that Z_(n+p)=Z_n for all n>=mu. For every n>=q, its q+1 coordinates take values in the q-element set Q, so at least two coordinates agree. Choose any n0>=mu. Select a<b with coordinates a and b equal in Z_n0. Periodicity gives those same coordinates equal in Z_(n0+kp) for every k>=0. Thus the selected pair collides on an infinite arithmetic progression of lengths. This selector is machine-dependent: its pair, mu, and p are obtained from the fixed transition system's finite orbit, and the argument does not give a uniform selector for machines varying with n.
